units.translation: 861 ff. the overall sense and the comparison are surely clear: the ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ denotes the Cretans who fight only at home among themselves. But ⟦3⟧ 'taking out the heart' does not even seem to have been the reading of the scholiast, who explains with ⟦4⟧. ⟦5⟧ however (Musgrave) does not lie very close to the features, and also gives nothing characteristic for the cocks; the other conjectures are equally unconvincing. So I keep (with Sidgwick) the transmitted text and only set the punctuation somewhat differently: ⟦6⟧ (⟦7⟧. 506 etc.) for ⟦8⟧ and comma before ⟦9⟧ and after ⟦10⟧, "as if you had taken out the heart of cocks, to implant it in the citizens (⟦11⟧.)."
⟦1⟧: cf. 355; in ⟦2⟧ the emphasis lies on ⟦3⟧.

V. 864 ⟦1⟧ the scholiast explains with ⟦2⟧; cf. ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧, according to Triclinius = ⟦5⟧; ⟦6⟧ ⟦7⟧, where no other meaning than 'utterly' is possible. This fits also in the Agamemnon; here this and that, also to what follows: "so much the more will mighty desire for glory inflame the hearts". The pride of the fighter of Marathon comes out here, as also below 913 ff. A. can also think of the battles with Boeotians and Chalcidians; of the civil strife, when Cleomenes occupied the citadel, he had experienced something as a boy, and upon these had quickly followed those heavy battles. ⟦8⟧ ⟦9⟧ B, ⟦10⟧. ⟦11⟧ ⟦12⟧. —

Chorus 870—880, antistrophe ⟦1⟧. The chorus still does not react, but repeats even now what was last presented.
Shorter repetition of what has just been said in detail.
⟦1⟧ 882 with ⟦2⟧ as at 100, ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧ with ⟦5⟧, ⟦6⟧ with ⟦7⟧; a kind of passive sense tends to be present (Wecklein).
⟦1⟧: see on 775. ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧, of whom ⟦5⟧; here of the rejected stranger. That they have been rejected by her, at least that Athena wants to make it impossible for them to say.
